claims.newSentence: In the UK its licensed uses, according to the summary of product characteristics (SmPC), are the symptomatic treatment of allergic rhinitis and of chronic idiopathic urticaria.
MedlinePlus, a US source, lists loratadine (Claritin) among antihistamines that cause less sleepiness than others.
When someone meets something they are allergic to, the body releases histamine, a chemical involved in the allergic reaction.
The NHS says loratadine works by blocking the effects of histamine, which reduces allergy symptoms.
The NHS says loratadine is much less likely to make people sleepy than some other antihistamines, although some people still feel slightly sleepy.
If drowsy, the NHS advises not driving, riding a bike or using tools or machinery until fully alert and awake.

The NHS says to call 999 for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, very fast or struggling breathing, a tight throat or trouble swallowing, skin, lips or tongue turning blue, grey or pale, sudden confusion or drowsiness, or fainting.
MedlinePlus, a US source, lists rash, hives, itching, trouble breathing or swallowing, or swelling of the face, lips or throat as reasons to call a doctor right away.
In the UK, NHS 111 or the GP the same day is the route for urgent advice that is not an emergency.
One UK patient leaflet describes dizziness and nausea as very rare effects and advises contacting a doctor if fits occur.
The NHS says loratadine can be taken in pregnancy and advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor.
Its antihistamines page says loratadine is usually recommended if an antihistamine is needed in pregnancy.
The UK SmPC reports more than 1000 exposed outcomes showing no malformation or foetal toxicity, yet says it is preferable as a precaution to avoid loratadine in pregnancy.
For breastfeeding, the NHS says only very small amounts of loratadine get into breast milk.
The UK SmPC takes a more cautious line, saying loratadine is excreted in breast milk and that its use in breastfeeding women is not recommended.
The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service reports that occasional cases of reduced milk supply have been described with loratadine.
According to the NHS, loratadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.
The SmPC notes that inhibitors of the liver enzymes CYP3A4 or CYP2D6 could raise loratadine levels.

The NHS says to tell a pharmacist or doctor about other medicines, including ones bought without a prescription, and names amiodarone, cimetidine, erythromycin and any medicine that causes drowsiness, dry mouth or difficulty peeing.
The leaflet advises that people with rare hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take the tablets.
The leaflet says the tablets have not been shown to add to the effects of an alcoholic drink, but the NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol because it can make a person sleepy.
On long-term use, the NHS says loratadine is unlikely to do harm but is best taken only for as long as needed.
It is described as non-drowsy, because the NHS says it is much less likely to cause sleepiness than some other antihistamines.
The NHS says loratadine can be taken in pregnancy and advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor.
The UK SmPC prefers avoiding it in pregnancy as a precaution, despite reassuring data.
The NHS says only very small amounts reach breast milk, while the SmPC does not recommend its use in breastfeeding women.
According to the NHS, loratadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.
The leaflet says loratadine has not been shown to add to the effects of an alcoholic drink.
